children: Rising rates may nudge Japanese companies to bring home their $5.3 trln in overseas portfolio investments. So far, however, it's global investors who are snapping up Sanae Takaichi’s mushrooming debt. It belies the idea of bond vigilantes expecting a Japanese fiscal crisis.
Full view will be published shortly.
Follow Jon Sindreu on X and LinkedIn.

The Japanese yen climbed to a seven-month high against the U.S. dollar on September 8, as traders unwound earlier bets against the currency. Markets increasingly believe that the Bank of Japan could raise interest rates at a faster pace, following comments from Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama and U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Japanese 10-year government yields, which had risen above 3% on September 2, have since retreated.

On September 2, Norway’s $2.2 trillion wealth fund, managed by Norges Bank Investment Management, proposed increasing its allocations to Japanese government bonds, alongside a reduction of its holdings of other developed nations’ sovereign debt.
As of 0800 GMT on September 10, $1 bought 153.42 yen. 10-year Japanese government yields last traded at 2.911%.
